newsitem.title: UK: British government to give queen travel allowance.
newsitem.headline: British government to give queen travel allowance.

text.p: Prime Minister John Major on Wednesday outlined plans to give Britain's Queen Elizabeth a travel allowance -- probably amounting to well over 10 million pounds ($15.8 million) a year.
The money will be available to fund trips by the queen and other members of the Royal Family to the 3,000 official engagements they undertake in Britain and abroad each year.

The new allowance will cover the cost of the Royal Train and a squadron of aircraft devoted to serving royalty, but will also allow Buckingham Palace to arrange for royals to travel on commercial airlines and trains.
However, it will exclude the cost of the royal yacht Britannia, which is due to be decommissioned next year.
Major said the new allowance, which will replace a system under which government departments meet the cost of royal travel as part of their general spending, would help to control costs.
"The aim of the change is to have one focus -- the Royal Household -- responsible for securing the best value for money from this public money," he said in a written parliamentary answer.
Major said that since the Royal Household took over responsibility from the government for the upkeep of royal palaces in 1991, cost savings of over 25 percent in real terms had been achieved.
Government officials said royal travel costs the British taxpayer some nine million pounds ($14.2 million) a year.
But they said the new allowance would include extra cash for capital spending and for paying for the use of runways and control towers which at present are excluded from the cost calculations.
The Queen travelled on a commercial airliner for the first time late last year when she flew Air New Zealand to the Auckland summit of Commonwealth heads of government.
The entire first class cabin of a jumbo jet was refurbished to enable her and her party to travel in the comfort to which they are accustomed.
